content: The presence of cyanobacteria in source waters can be effectively managed by minimizing bloom formation and positioning raw water intake points away from bloom areas. This approach reduces the need for extensive treatment processes to remove cyanotoxins. Drinking water treatment methods that remove particles, such as soil filtration, slow sand or riverbank filtration, conventional water treatment (coagulation, flocculation, and filtration), or dissolved air flotation, are effective in removing cell-bound cyanotoxins (CYNs). Additionally, soil, slow sand, and riverbank filtration can also remove dissolved cyanotoxins. It is crucial to optimize these processes to target both cell removal and dissolved toxin elimination. During pre-oxidation and conventional treatment, it is important to avoid cell rupture and toxin release while addressing the typically high proportion of dissolved CYNs. Chlorination and ozonation, when applied at sufficiently high doses and contact times, are effective in degrading dissolved CYNs. However, elevated organic carbon levels during bloom situations can significantly increase disinfectant demand. Chlorine dioxide and chloramine are ineffective for degrading CYNs. Granular activated carbon (GAC) and powdered activated carbon (PAC) can effectively remove dissolved CYNs, with their efficacy depending on factors such as the type of activated carbon, contact times (for PAC), flow rates (for GAC), and water quality. Given the complexity of bloom-related challenges, periodic validation of treatment efficacy during bloom events and under specific local conditions is essential. Preventing bloom occurrence and avoiding intake from affected areas remains the preferred strategy. The chemical 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid) is a systemic herbicide used to control broad-leaved weeds, including aquatic weeds. Commercial formulations include the free acid, alkali and amine salts, and esters, with the esters rapidly hydrolyzing to the free acid. 2,4-D is chemically stable and biodegrades quickly in the environment. Residues in food are typically low, rarely exceeding a few tens of micrograms per kilogram. The guideline value for 2,4-D in drinking water is based on its rapid hydrolysis to the free acid and its allocation to water consumption. The Joint FAO/WHO Meeting on Pesticide Residues (JMPR) concluded that the available data are insufficient to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of 2,4-D. It also determined that 2,4-D and its salts and esters are not genotoxic, and their toxicity is comparable to that of the free acid. The chemical DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane) is a persistent organic pollutant with restricted or banned use in many countries, though it is still employed in some regions for vector control against diseases like malaria. DDT and its metabolites are resistant to degradation and persist in the environment. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified DDT as a non-genotoxic carcinogen in rodents and a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B) based on sufficient evidence of liver tumors in experimental animals. The benefits of DDT use in vector control programs outweigh the potential health risks from its presence in drinking water. The chemical 1,2-dibromo-3-chloropropane (DBCP) is a soil fumigant with high water solubility. It has been classified as a Group 2B carcinogen by IARC due to sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity in animals. DBCP is also a reproductive toxicant in humans and laboratory animals and has been found to be genotoxic in most in vitro and in vivo assays. Recent epidemiological evidence suggests increased cancer mortality in individuals exposed to high levels of DBCP. The chemical 1,2-dibromoethane (ethylene dibromide) is used as a lead scavenger in gasoline and as a fumigant for soil, grains, and fruits. Its use has declined significantly with the phasing out of leaded gasoline and agricultural applications. IARC has classified 1,2-dibromoethane as a Group 2A carcinogen (probably carcinogenic to humans) based on sufficient evidence of carcinogenicity in animals. It is a genotoxic carcinogen in rodents, with tumor induction likely involving biotransformation to active metabolites that bind to DNA. Dichloroacetic acid (DCA), a byproduct of water chlorination, has been classified as a Group 2B carcinogen by IARC due to sufficient evidence of liver tumors in experimental animals. The available data on its genotoxicity are inconclusive, and its carcinogenicity may involve multiple mechanisms, including glycogen deposition, peroxisome proliferation, and DNA hypomethylation. Dichlorobenzenes (DCBs) are used in industry and domestic products. The 1,4-DCB is classified as a Group 2B carcinogen by IARC due to evidence of renal tumors in rats and liver tumors in mice. The 1,2-DCB is of low acute toxicity and is not considered genotoxic or carcinogenic. There is insufficient toxicological data on 1,3-DCB to propose a guideline value. 1,1-Dichloroethane is used as a chemical intermediate and solvent. It is rapidly metabolized in mammals and is of low acute toxicity. Limited data suggest it is not genotoxic, and there is no conclusive evidence of carcinogenicity. Due to the limited toxicity database, no guideline value is proposed. 1,2-Dichloroethane is used in the production of vinyl chloride and other chemicals. It is classified as a Group 2B carcinogen by IARC due to evidence of tumor induction in animals. It is potentially genotoxic, with toxicity targets including the immune system, central nervous system, liver, and kidneys. 1,1-Dichloroethene (vinylidene chloride) is used in polymer production and is occasionally found in drinking water. It is a central nervous system depressant and may cause liver and kidney toxicity. IARC has classified it as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans). It has shown genotoxicity in vitro but not in vivo. 1,2-Dichloroethene exists in cis and trans forms, with the cis isomer more commonly found as a water contaminant. Both isomers may have some genotoxic activity, but there is no information on their carcinogenicity. The cis isomer is more rapidly metabolized than the trans isomer. Dichloromethane (methylene chloride) is widely used as a solvent. It is classified as a Group 2B carcinogen by IARC, though the evidence suggests it is not a genotoxic carcinogen. 1,2-Dichloropropane (1,2-DCP) is used as a fumigant and solvent. IARC has classified it as Group 3 (not classifiable as to its carcinogenicity to humans) due to limited evidence in animals and insufficient data in humans.
